title: Body Fluids and Circulation
description: Grade 11 Biology: blood and its components, blood groups and lymph, the structure of the human heart, the cardiac cycle and double circulation, and circulatory disorders.

topics.title: Blood, Blood Groups and Lymph
topics.concept:
Cells deep inside the body cannot get food and oxygen directly from outside, so the body uses a fluid transport system. The main body fluid is blood, a special connective tissue made of a liquid part (plasma) and cells suspended in it.

  • Plasma — the pale yellow liquid (about 55% of blood); it is mostly water and carries dissolved food, salts, hormones, wastes and proteins.
  • Red blood cells (RBCs / erythrocytes) — contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen; they have no nucleus when mature and are made in the bone marrow.
  • White blood cells (WBCs / leucocytes) — fight germs and defend the body (immunity).
  • Platelets (thrombocytes) — help the blood to clot and stop bleeding from a wound.

Human blood is of four blood groups — A, B, AB and O — based on antigens on the RBCs. Group O is the "universal donor" and AB the "universal recipient." Another important grouping is the Rh factor: people are Rh-positive or Rh-negative. Matching blood groups is essential before a transfusion.

Lymph is another body fluid — a colourless fluid that leaks out of blood capillaries into the tissues, bathes the cells, and is collected by lymph vessels and returned to the blood. It carries nutrients and fights infection but has no RBCs.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the four components of blood.
examples.solution:
Blood is plasma plus cells.

  • Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
examples.answer: Plasma, red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs) and platelets.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the function of platelets?
examples.solution:
They act at wounds.

  • Platelets help the blood to clot and stop bleeding.
examples.answer: Platelets help the blood to clot and stop bleeding from wounds.

examples.problem: Example 3: Which blood group is the universal donor, and which is the universal recipient?
examples.solution:
Recall the special groups.

  • O is the universal donor.
  • AB is the universal recipient.
examples.answer: Group O is the universal donor; group AB is the universal recipient.

recap:
• Blood = plasma (liquid, ~55%) + RBCs (haemoglobin/O₂), WBCs (defence), platelets (clotting).
  • Blood groups: A, B, AB, O; O = universal donor, AB = universal recipient; plus Rh factor (+/-).
  • Lymph: colourless tissue fluid; carries nutrients, fights infection; no RBCs; returns to blood.

quiz.q: The component of blood that helps it clot is the:
The universal donor blood group is:
quiz.explanation: Group O is the universal donor.

topics.title: The Human Heart and Circulation
topics.concept:
The heart is a muscular organ, about the size of a fist, that pumps blood throughout the body. It lies in the chest between the two lungs and is made of a special muscle (cardiac muscle) that never tires. The human heart has four chambers: two upper atria (auricles) that receive blood, and two lower ventricles that pump blood out. The thick-walled left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body. Valves between the chambers and at the exits keep the blood flowing in one direction only and prevent back-flow.

Humans have a double circulation — blood passes through the heart twice in one complete round:

  • Pulmonary circulation — the heart pumps de-oxygenated blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen, and returns it to the heart.
  • Systemic circulation — the heart then pumps the oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body, and the de-oxygenated blood returns to the heart.

This keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood completely separate, which is very efficient. The blood vessels are: arteries (carry blood away from the heart, usually oxygenated, thick-walled), veins (carry blood back to the heart, have valves) and capillaries (tiny, thin-walled vessels where exchange of materials with cells happens).

One full sequence of the heart relaxing and contracting is the cardiac cycle; the contraction is called systole and the relaxation diastole. The familiar "lub-dub" heart sounds are made by the valves closing. A healthy adult heart beats about 70–72 times per minute.

examples.problem: Example 1: How many chambers does the human heart have, and what are they called?
examples.solution:
Recall the structure.

  • Four chambers.
  • Two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).
examples.answer: Four chambers — two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the role of the valves in the heart?
examples.solution:
Valves control flow direction.

  • They keep blood flowing in one direction and prevent back-flow.
examples.answer: Valves ensure blood flows in only one direction and prevent it from flowing backward.

examples.solution:
Blood passes through the heart twice.

  • Pulmonary circulation (heart → lungs → heart).
  • Systemic circulation (heart → body → heart).
examples.answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice per round — pulmonary (to lungs) and systemic (to body).

recap:
• Heart: 4 chambers — 2 atria (receive), 2 ventricles (pump); valves prevent back-flow; cardiac muscle.
  • Double circulation: pulmonary (heart→lungs→heart) + systemic (heart→body→heart); keeps O₂-rich/poor blood separate.
  • Vessels: arteries (away, thick), veins (back, valves), capillaries (exchange).
  • Cardiac cycle: systole (contract) + diastole (relax); ~70–72 beats/min; "lub-dub" = valves closing.

quiz.q: The lower pumping chambers of the heart are the:
quiz.explanation: The ventricles are the lower chambers that pump blood out.

quiz.q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are:
quiz.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

topics.title: Circulatory Disorders and Heart Health
topics.concept:
The heart and blood vessels can develop problems, especially with age and an unhealthy lifestyle. Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, so understanding and preventing it matters. Some important circulatory disorders:

  • High blood pressure (hypertension) — the blood pushes too hard against the artery walls. It often has no symptoms but damages the heart, brain and kidneys over time. Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm Hg.
  • Coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis) — the arteries supplying the heart muscle get narrowed by deposits of fat and cholesterol, reducing blood flow to the heart.
  • Heart attack (myocardial infarction) — a part of the heart muscle is damaged because its blood supply is suddenly blocked.
  • Angina — chest pain that occurs when the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen.

Common risk factors include smoking, a fatty diet, obesity, lack of exercise, stress, diabetes and a family history of heart disease. The good news is that much heart disease is preventable. To keep the heart healthy: eat a balanced diet low in saturated fat and salt, exercise regularly, maintain a healthy weight, avoid smoking and excess alcohol, manage stress, and get regular health check-ups (including blood pressure). These simple habits, started young, greatly lower the lifelong risk of heart disease.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is hypertension, and what is the normal blood pressure value?
examples.solution:
It is about blood pressure.

  • Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure.
  • Normal is about 120/80 mm Hg.
examples.answer: Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure; normal is about 120/80 mm Hg.

examples.solution:
It involves the heart's blood supply.

  • The blood supply to part of the heart muscle is suddenly blocked.
  • That part of the muscle is damaged.
examples.answer: A heart attack happens when the blood supply to part of the heart muscle is suddenly blocked, damaging that muscle.

examples.problem: Example 3: List three habits that help keep the heart healthy.
examples.solution:
Focus on prevention.

  • Eat a balanced low-fat, low-salt diet; exercise regularly.
  • Avoid smoking (and manage weight/stress).
examples.answer: Eat a healthy low-fat/low-salt diet, exercise regularly, and avoid smoking (plus manage weight and stress).

recap:
• Hypertension: high blood pressure (normal ~120/80 mm Hg); silent but damaging.
  • Atherosclerosis: fatty deposits narrow arteries; heart attack: blocked supply damages heart muscle; angina: chest pain from low oxygen.
  • Risk factors: smoking, fatty diet, obesity, inactivity, stress, diabetes.
  • Prevention: healthy diet, exercise, no smoking, weight/stress control, check-ups.

quiz.q: Normal human blood pressure is about:
quiz.explanation: Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm Hg.

quiz.q: Narrowing of the heart's arteries by fatty deposits is:
quiz.explanation: Atherosclerosis is the narrowing of arteries by fat/cholesterol deposits.

questions.q: The liquid part of blood is called:
questions.explanation: Plasma is the pale-yellow liquid part of blood.

questions.q: Oxygen is carried mainly by:
questions.explanation: RBCs carry oxygen using haemoglobin.

questions.q: Cells that defend the body against germs are:
questions.explanation: WBCs (leucocytes) provide immunity/defence.

questions.q: Blood clotting is helped by:
questions.explanation: Platelets help the blood to clot.

questions.q: The universal recipient blood group is:
questions.explanation: Group AB is the universal recipient.

questions.q: A colourless body fluid with no RBCs that bathes the cells is:
questions.explanation: Lymph is the colourless tissue fluid with no RBCs.

questions.q: The human heart has how many chambers?
questions.explanation: The human heart has four chambers.

questions.q: The upper chambers of the heart are the:
questions.explanation: The atria are the upper receiving chambers.

questions.q: Heart valves mainly:
questions.explanation: Valves keep blood flowing one way and prevent back-flow.

questions.q: Passage of blood through the heart twice in one round is called:
questions.explanation: Humans have double circulation (pulmonary + systemic).

questions.q: Vessels that carry blood back to the heart are:
questions.explanation: Veins carry blood back to the heart and have valves.

questions.q: Exchange of materials between blood and cells happens in the:
questions.explanation: Thin-walled capillaries allow exchange with tissues.

questions.q: The contraction phase of the heart is called:
questions.explanation: Systole is contraction; diastole is relaxation.

questions.q: Persistently high blood pressure is called:
questions.explanation: Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure.

questions.q: Sudden blockage of blood supply to part of the heart muscle is a:
questions.explanation: A blocked supply causing heart-muscle damage is a heart attack.

questions.q: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must:
options: Pump blood to the whole body
questions.explanation: Pumping blood all around the body needs the greatest force, so its wall is thickest.

questions.q: Double circulation is efficient because it keeps:
questions.explanation: Separating oxygenated and de-oxygenated blood ensures tissues get fully oxygen-rich blood.

questions.q: Veins have valves but most arteries do not because:
options: Vein blood flows slowly at low pressure and could flow backward
questions.explanation: Low-pressure venous return needs valves to stop backflow; high-pressure arterial flow does not.

questions.q: Before a blood transfusion, blood groups must be matched to avoid:
questions.explanation: Mismatched groups cause the recipient's antibodies to clump the donor cells — a dangerous reaction.

questions.q: Atherosclerosis raises the risk of a heart attack because narrowed arteries:
options: Reduce blood flow to the heart muscle
questions.explanation: Fatty deposits choke the heart's blood supply, so a blockage can starve the muscle of oxygen.

questions.q: The 'lub-dub' heart sounds are produced by:
questions.explanation: The two sounds come from the heart valves snapping shut during the cardiac cycle.
